Here's the page, written to drop straight into the welcome pack and the Facebook group. I've left the birth line number and a couple of details as blanks for you to fill in before it goes out.

---

# Helping Your Midwife Find You

**Riverside Community Midwives — Welcome Pack**
*This page is also on our Riverside mums and dads Facebook group. Screenshot it and send it to your partner, your mum, whoever is coming to the birth with you.*

---

Hello. I'm one of the community midwives on the Riverside team, and I have a confession to make: **I have been lost.** Not once. Not twice. There was a 20-minute lap around a block of flats in Everton that turned into a treasure hunt, and I have met a lovely gentleman in a dressing gown who made me a cup of tea and handed me a Jammie Dodger when I accidentally knocked on his door looking for Flat 13.

So this page is my apology to you, in writing. Follow it and you'll save me (and your partner) the 3am scenic tour of your neighbourhood. You'll also get us to your door while you actually need us.

Read it now, when you've got a cup of tea and nobody's in labour. Then stick the checklist on the fridge.

## Before the birth: the 37 week rule

Home birth cover on the Riverside team starts at **37 weeks**. Before 37 weeks, if baby comes, you go to the hospital. That's the rule — and it's a rule we will be quietly but very firmly reminding you about at booking, at 36 weeks, and probably at 37 weeks as well.

If you think you're in labour before 37 weeks: **phone the birth line.** Don't sit at home worrying, and don't assume we'll just turn up.

## When labour starts: phone the birth line

**Riverside Birth Line: ____________________**
*(fill this in before printing — and write it on the fridge checklist too)*

- **Phone it when labour starts**, not when the contractions are so bad you can't talk. We'd much rather come early and sit with you for an hour than miss you entirely.
- **Ring the birth line, not a midwife's personal mobile.** The line goes to whoever is on call that night. If you ring a personal number and she's asleep, or on a bus, or in the middle of a birth with someone else, you'll be left waiting — and so will we.
- If you can't get through, keep ringing. Somebody will pick up.
- **If it's an emergency** — heavy bleeding, a fit, the cord showing, or you feel very unwell — **call 999 straight away**, then tell us. Don't wait for us.
- **If baby arrives before we do:** put baby on your chest, skin to skin, keep them warm, and phone us again. We will still come.

## How we'll find you

**House numbers and names.** Please make sure your **house number is clearly visible** from the road, especially if it's dark. If your home only has a name — "Rosemary Cottage" — that is a lovely name and we will love it, but at 3am in a terrace we need the number as well. Put it on the door, on the gate, on a card in the window, anywhere you can.

**Send us a pin.** Two easy ways to help:

- **what3words.** Write the three words on a piece of paper by your front door and send them to the birth line. Three words is about as precise as three metres. Send the *words*, not just the app — whoever's on call may not have it.
- **A pin on WhatsApp.** Send a map pin to the birth line phone number, then add a note like "blue door, green bin, gate on the left."

**Porch light on.** Please put your porch light on before we arrive. Winter streets in Liverpool all look exactly the same: same dark hedges, same orange sodium light, same drizzle. A lit porch is the single kindest thing you can do for a midwife on a night shift.

**Lock or leave the key.** Leave the door unlocked, or have a key ready, or tell us where the spare is. If you're on the phone with us and can't come down, we need to be able to get in. (Not under the mat, please — we'll find it, but only after we've checked the entire porch.)

**Tell us the route in.** If your street is a maze, one-way, or has a railway line or bridge in the way, tell us. "Turn left at the shop with the red awning" is genuinely useful information.

## Parking: two of us, two cars

Two midwives usually come for the birth, and we usually come in **separate cars** — so please try to keep **two parking spaces free** outside your house.

We also carry a lot: the big bag, gas and air cylinders for pain relief, and sometimes the birthing pool kit. Those cylinders are heavy and our arms are already tired by the time we reach your door. Parking right outside saves us five minutes and a hundred yards of wheeling equipment.

**Permit zones.** Some streets around **Anfield and Kensington** are in a council parking permit zone. If yours is:

- **Ask Liverpool City Council about a visitor parking permit** before the birth — much easier to sort when you're not in labour.
- Or ask the permit holder to **leave a valid permit clearly on the dashboard**, and tell us that's what it is.
- We have had tickets before. We would very much like to stop that happening.

Also check for **double yellow lines** and resident-only bays. If we can, we won't block your neighbours' driveways.

## Inside: clearing a path

This is the bit people feel bad about. **You're not being told off — you're making room for a whole delivery team.**

- **Hallway and stairs clear**, from the front door right through to the room you want to birth in, and ideally to the bathroom.
- **Shoes off** (or slippers on). We need to move fast and not slip.
- **No washing basket in the hallway.** Lovely laundry, terrible obstacle course.
- **No Lego, no mountain of shoes, no bike, no pram** if it can live somewhere else. We'll never complain about your mess, but a clear path means we don't have to move a mountain to reach you.
- **Think about where the pool goes**, if you want one. We need space for it and a hose that reaches.

## Pets

We love dogs. Genuinely. Some of us will not be able to resist a friendly face.

But please put **pets in another room** before we arrive and keep them there through the birth. It's not that your dog is bad — it's that you shouldn't have to manage an excited animal and a contraction at the same time, and because a dog near gas cylinders and a newborn is not a good combination. Fetch the biscuit, shut the door, don't feel guilty.

*(One of our team, Pippin, would like it noted that she is excellent with dogs, and that the time she jumped up during a visit and nearly put the Entonox through a window was an accident. She has been told to sit down.)*

## A few things we've learned the hard way

All true, all in the hope you don't have to learn them the hard way:

- **The balloon idea is the best idea ever.** One family put balloons on their gate, like it was a party, and we found it straight away. If you've got bunting, fairy lights, a banner, a doormat that says something cheerful — use it. We will be drawn to it like moths.
- **Number order is not always number order.** We went looking for Flat 13 and found Flat 14 in a completely different building. The dad eventually waved a tea towel out of the window, which was the actual reason we found the right one. (Tea towel signals: officially recognised. Unofficially: brilliant.)
- **Sat nav sent us to a chippy.** Not a café, not a corner shop — a chippy. Because the house was called "Rosemary Cottage" and had no number. Please: numbers. Numbers everywhere.
- **We have knocked on the wrong door.** A very nice man in a dressing gown gave me a Jammie Dodger. Sir, if you're reading this: we're sorry, and thank you.

## You're not a guest — we're coming as family

I grew up hearing that in the Philippines, a midwife is like family. That's exactly how we want to be with you. This is your house, your birth, your room. We'll knock before we come in. We'll ask before we do anything. We'll tell you what's happening and what's coming next. And afterwards, when you're sitting there with a new person in your arms, we'll still be the ones tidying up and making you a cup of tea.

## Fridge checklist

Print this, stick it on the fridge, and tick it off together in the last few weeks. Post a photo on the Facebook group and we'll send you a heart emoji.

- [ ] **House number clearly visible from the road** (and on the door itself)
- [ ] **House name AND number** written down if your home has both
- [ ] **Two parking spaces** kept free outside the house
- [ ] **Council visitor parking permit** sorted, if you're in an Anfield or Kensington permit zone
- [ ] **Permit or pass on the dashboard**, ready to go
- [ ] **Porch light works** — and the bulb isn't dead
- [ ] **Key ready**, or door unlocked, or spare key location written down here: ____________________
- [ ] **what3words** written down by the door or saved on your phone
- [ ] **Map pin sent** to the birth line with a note about the door/bin/gate
- [ ] **Hallway and stairs clear** — shoes off, washing basket moved, Lego relocated
- [ ] **Room chosen** for the birth, with space for the pool if you want one
- [ ] **Pets sorted** — food, water, and a plan to shut them in another room
- [ ] **Phone charged**, good signal, birth line number saved
- [ ] **Food in the house** for you, and something for the midwives (we will be grateful)

---

**A few things to sort before it goes out:**

- The birth line number is a blank in two places (the main section and the checklist) — worth printing in bold on the fridge copy so it's readable from the door.
- I've described the Anfield and Kensington permit zones in general terms rather than quoting council rules or timescales, since those change. Worth a quick check with the council's visitor permit team, and you may want to add the current cost and how long they take to arrive — that's usually the bit that catches people out.
- I've added an emergency 999 line (bleeding, fit, cord showing, feeling very unwell) and a "baby arrives before we do" section, since both come up in training and neither was in your notes.
- If you want the funny bits to land on Facebook, the balloon line and the Jammie Dodger line are the ones that tend to get shared in the comments.
